indicator.name: CoinMarketCap Crypto Market Metrics
indicator.description: A market-wide daily snapshot from CoinMarketCap containing aggregate cryptocurrency market capitalization, trading volume, market-share measures, sector-level market capitalization and volume, derivatives activity, market growth rates, and ecosystem activity statistics. The dataset provides a broad view of crypto-market size, liquidity, market structure, capital distribution, and changes in market activity within a single observation.
indicator.use: Monitor the overall size, liquidity, composition, activity, and structural changes of the cryptocurrency market using CoinMarketCap's aggregate market metrics.
indicator.purpose: Provide a consolidated market-wide snapshot for understanding total crypto-market capitalization, trading activity, Bitcoin and Ethereum market share, altcoin and DeFi market size, stablecoin liquidity, derivatives activity, and changes in the broader crypto ecosystem.
indicator.significance: CoinMarketCap Crypto Market Metrics provides broad market context that can be used to interpret changes across individual crypto assets and specialized indicators. Total market capitalization measures the aggregate value of the cryptocurrency market, while 24-hour spot trading volume provides a measure of market activity and liquidity. Altcoin market capitalization and volume help isolate activity outside Bitcoin, while Bitcoin and Ethereum dominance measure their respective shares of the total cryptocurrency market and can provide context for capital distribution and rotation. DeFi market capitalization and volume provide visibility into decentralized-finance activity, while stablecoin market capitalization and volume provide context for the size and activity of crypto-native liquidity instruments. Derivatives volume provides a measure of activity in crypto derivatives markets. The dataset also includes daily percentage changes in total market capitalization, total volume, DeFi activity, stablecoin activity, and derivatives activity, allowing the system to identify rapid changes in market conditions. Active cryptocurrency, market-pair, and exchange counts provide additional context for the size and breadth of the crypto ecosystem. These metrics can be analyzed alongside asset prices, market breadth, volatility, derivatives positioning, funding rates, stablecoin indicators, Bitcoin dominance, DeFi indicators, and macroeconomic conditions to identify changes in liquidity, market participation, capital rotation, and broader crypto-market regimes.

indicator.name: Alternative.me Crypto Fear & Greed Index
indicator.description: A daily composite index from Alternative.me measuring crypto-market sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, where lower values represent greater fear and higher values represent greater greed. Alternative.me derives the index from multiple sentiment-related inputs, including Bitcoin volatility, market momentum and volume, social media activity, surveys, Bitcoin dominance, and Google Trends. Alternative.me's published methodology currently identifies the index as Bitcoin-focused.
indicator.use: Track daily changes in aggregate crypto-market sentiment using Alternative.me's composite Fear & Greed Index and its fear-to-greed classification.
indicator.purpose: Provide a standardized daily measure of market sentiment that can be used to identify shifts between fear, neutrality, and greed in the crypto market.
indicator.significance: The Alternative.me Crypto Fear & Greed Index combines multiple market and sentiment signals into a single 0-to-100 measure. Alternative.me's published methodology assigns 25% weight to volatility, 25% to market momentum and volume, 15% to social media, 15% to surveys, 10% to Bitcoin dominance, and 10% to Google Trends, although Alternative.me currently states that its surveys are paused. The index therefore captures several dimensions of market behavior rather than directly measuring investor sentiment through a single survey. It can be analyzed alongside price trends, volatility, trading volume, derivatives positioning, funding rates, market breadth, Bitcoin dominance, and other sentiment indicators to provide broader context for changes in crypto-market conditions.

indicator.name: CoinMarketCap Altcoin Season Index
indicator.description: A daily CoinMarketCap index measuring the relative performance of major altcoins versus Bitcoin over a rolling 90-day period. The index uses the top 100 eligible coins ranked on CoinMarketCap, excluding stablecoins and wrapped or asset-backed tokens, and scales the proportion of coins outperforming Bitcoin to a 0-to-100 index.
indicator.use: Track the degree to which major altcoins are outperforming or underperforming Bitcoin over a rolling 90-day period and identify shifts between Bitcoin-dominant and altcoin-dominant market regimes.
indicator.purpose: Provide a standardized measure of altcoin market breadth relative to Bitcoin and identify broad changes in relative performance across the cryptocurrency market.
indicator.significance: The CoinMarketCap Altcoin Season Index measures market breadth by comparing the rolling 90-day performance of the top 100 eligible coins on CoinMarketCap against Bitcoin. Stablecoins and wrapped or asset-backed tokens are excluded from the constituent set. The index reflects the proportion of these coins outperforming Bitcoin and is scaled from 1 to 100. Values above 75 indicate Altcoin Season, while values at or below 25 indicate Bitcoin Season. The index therefore measures the breadth of altcoin outperformance rather than sentiment directly: a high value means a large share of major altcoins have outperformed Bitcoin over the measurement period, while a low value means relatively few have done so. It can be analyzed alongside Bitcoin dominance, altcoin market capitalization, market breadth, liquidity, trading volume, and crypto-market sentiment to provide context for changes in market regime and capital rotation.

indicator.name: Bitcoin Spot ETF Market
indicator.description: A daily measure of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF market activity, including aggregate net capital flows, traded value, net assets, and cumulative net flows. The indicator provides a view of capital entering or leaving the Bitcoin spot ETF market and the size and activity of the investment vehicles providing regulated market access to Bitcoin.
indicator.use: Track daily capital flows, trading activity, assets under management, and cumulative capital flows in the U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF market.
indicator.purpose: Provide a daily view of institutional and traditional-finance market participation in Bitcoin through regulated spot ETF vehicles and identify changes in capital allocation toward Bitcoin.
indicator.significance: Bitcoin spot ETF market data provides a direct view of capital flows and asset levels within regulated investment vehicles that give traditional investors access to Bitcoin. Net flow measures the daily net movement of capital into or out of the ETF market, while value traded measures ETF trading activity. Net assets indicate the aggregate size of assets held through the ETF vehicles, and cumulative net flow tracks the longer-term accumulation of capital flows since the measurement period began. Bitcoin ETF activity can provide important context for institutional and traditional-finance participation in Bitcoin and can be analyzed alongside Bitcoin price, Bitcoin dominance, derivatives positioning, open interest, funding rates, macroeconomic conditions, inflation expectations, interest rates, Treasury yields, liquidity conditions, and broader crypto-market sentiment. ETF flows should be interpreted as activity within the spot Bitcoin ETF market and should not be treated as a complete measure of all institutional Bitcoin ownership or total Bitcoin demand.

indicator.use: Track changes in Bitcoin futures open interest and positioning across dealers, asset managers, leveraged funds, other reportable traders, and nonreportable traders, including shifts in long, short, spreading, and net exposure.
indicator.purpose: Provide asset-specific visibility into how different classes of market participants are positioned in Bitcoin futures and how their exposure changes over time.

Changes in open interest reveal changes in futures-market participation, while changes in long and short positions show how each trader group is adjusting directional exposure. Separating trader classifications allows the intelligence system to distinguish institutional and leveraged positioning from dealer activity and aggregate nonreportable participation when analyzing Bitcoin market structure and sentiment.

highlights: US Government Moves $71M Bitcoin Stash After 6-Week Silence Published: 2026-10-06T23:50:20Z US Government Moves $71M Bitcoin Stash After 6-Week Silence US Government Moves $71M Bitcoin Stash After 6-Week Silence **On Tuesday, the U.S. government moved bitcoin for the first time since Aug. 26, with government-linked wallets shifting 833.6 BTC valued at just over $71 million. The coins trace back to two separate cases involving the Potapenko-Turogin fraud case and the 2016 Bitfinex hack.** * Wallets managed by the U.S. Marshals, a DOJ agency, moved 833.6 BTC worth $71M, their first bitcoin transfer since Aug. 26. * Coinbase Prime entered the picture as government wallets tested BTC transfers tied to 2 major cases. * Uncle Sam still sits on a hefty 323,693.83 BTC stash valued at roughly $27.72 billion. Roughly around 11 a.m. Eastern time, the U.S. government shifted a large sum of bitcoin, alongside $31.63 million worth of BNB, from forfeited FTX wallets. Sani, the onchain analyst and operator of timechainindex.com, was the [first to discover the movements](https://x.com/TimechainIndex/status/2107496400263188525?s=20). He noted that the federal authorities shifted 0.00115539 BTC to Coinbase Prime in a test transfer and moved 264.86266831 BTC to a new wallet. “Most likely a test transaction before sending all the remaining coins,” Sani wrote on X. This specific stash was coins associated with the 2016 Bitfinex hack, which saw 120,000 BTC stolen from the exchange. The government managed to catch the hackers, Ilya Lichtenstein and [Heather Morgan](https://news.bitcoin.com/no-trump-did-not-commute-heather-razzlekhan-morgans-prison-sentence/), and confiscate around 94,636 BTC from the thieves years later. Following that transfer, the U.S. government’s wallets moved a test transfer of 0.127 BNB from the [FTX bankruptcy](https://news.bitcoin.com/from-a-32-billion-valuation-to-financial-troubles-an-in-depth-look-at-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx/) and then shifted a much larger 40,285.07 BNB. That move was then followed by a 568 BTC transaction with coins that derived from the Potapenko-Turogin fraud case. That case in particular involved two men who ran a fake cloud mining operation called Hashflare. The men, Sergei Potapenko and Ivan Turõgin, sold contracts of hashrate from data centers that held no real machines. Tuesday may have been a day for cleaning out some forfeited digital assets, though why the government chose this particular moment to move them remains anyone’s guess. [Arkham Intelligence data](https://arkm.com/explorer/entity/usg) and Sani’s account of the situation show that the sender chose to move the funds to Coinbase Prime. Coinbase has had a relationship with the U.S. government when it comes to managing digital assets. The exchange provides custody and advanced trading services to the U.S. Marshals Service. In the old days, the government used to rely on auctions to sell bitcoin caches that were seized, but these days, [law enforcement](https://news.bitcoin.com/crypto-news/clarity-act-section-604-sheriffs-blockchain-association/) authorities work directly with Coinbase to handle its “Class 1” digital assets. After the 833.6 BTC moved on Tuesday, the U.S. government still holds 323,693.83 BTC worth $27.72 billion.

results.title: US Government's Bitcoin Move: Restitution and the Future of Crypto Seizures (2026)
highlights: The crypto world is buzzing with news of the US government moving 264 Bitcoin (worth a cool $23 million) to Coinbase as part of the Bitfinex restitution saga. But here’s the thing: this isn’t your typical government sell-off. Personally, I think this move is far more intriguing than it seems at first glance. What makes this particularly fascinating is that it’s not about liquidation but rather a long-overdue return of assets to their rightful owner. If you take a step back and think about it, this is a rare instance where the government is acting as a custodian rather than a seller, and that’s a significant shift in how we perceive its role in the crypto space. A Homecoming, Not a Fire Sale Let’s break this down. The Bitcoin in question comes from the infamous 2016 Bitfinex hack, one of the largest crypto heists in history. In 2022, federal authorities recovered about 94,636 BTC after arresting the culprits, Ilya Lichtenstein and Heather Morgan. Fast forward to October 2026, and a chunk of that stash is being moved to Coinbase Prime, the institutional arm of the exchange. highlights: Peter Thiel-backed Founders Fund leads a $5 million token buy in crypto collateral protocol Anvil Peter Thiel-backed Founders Fund leads a $5 million token buy in crypto collateral protocol Anvil Pantera Capital and Bullish also participated in the ANVL purchase as Anvil rolls out software designed to make its collateral protocol easier for businesses to integrate. - Founders Fund led a $5 million purchase of Anvil governance tokens, with participation from Pantera Capital, Theta Blockchain Ventures, Bullish and Protoscale Capital. - Anvil launched a software development kit intended to help businesses and financial institutions integrate its digital-asset collateral technology without writing blockchain code. - Unlike conventional decentralized finance lenders, Anvil uses collateral to guarantee financial commitments without requiring the provider to take out a loan or pay interest. Founders Fund has led a $5 million purchase of governance tokens in Anvil, a decentralized finance protocol focused on digital-asset collateral, as the project rolls out new tools aimed at bringing its technology to businesses and financial institutions. Pantera Capital, Theta Blockchain Ventures, Bullish and Protoscale Capital also participated in the purchase of ANVL tokens, according to a Monday announcement. The terms and valuation of the transaction were not disclosed. Anvil told CoinDesk the tokens came from its existing treasury rather than being newly issued. Anvil, built on Ethereum, is designed to allow digital assets to be used as collateral for financial commitments, including payments and credit. Anvil Research Labs, a research and development company building enterprise tools for the protocol, also launched a software development kit (SDK) that it said will allow companies to integrate Anvil without having to write blockchain code. The ANVL tokens purchased by Founders Fund and the other investors provide governance rights over the protocol, allowing holders to participate in decisions about its development. Anvil is entering a part of decentralized finance where putting crypto up as collateral is already commonplace. DeFi lending protocols currently hold about $56 billion of assets, according to DefiLlama, with Aave and Morpho among the largest platforms. But Anvil is aiming to put crypto collateral to a different use. Conventional DeFi lenders generally allow users to deposit assets as collateral and borrow against them, paying interest and potentially facing liquidation if the value of their collateral falls. Anvil instead uses collateral to guarantee a financial commitment without necessarily creating a loan. Its core product is an onchain version of a letter of credit: assets are reserved to guarantee payment to another party and can be claimed if the commitment isn't met, according to a CoinDesk Research report. The arrangement doesn't require the collateral provider to borrow money or pay interest simply to create the guarantee.

results.title: Ethereum gas is at 0.1 Gwei. Here is why the network feels like a ghost town - CryptoBuyingTips
highlights: Ethereum gas is at 0.1 Gwei. Here is why the network feels like a ghost town - Crypto Sigrid Voss · October 1, 2026 The crypto market is currently in a state of Greed, with the Fear & Greed Index sitting at 68. Prices are climbing, and the general sentiment is that we are in a risk-on environment. But if you look at the plumbing of the world's largest smart contract platform, the picture is different. Our live market metrics feed shows Ethereum gas is currently at 0.1 Gwei. For anyone who remembers paying a hundred dollars to move a few tokens during the 2021 NFT craze, this feels like a miracle. However, if you are wondering what does low ethereum gas mean for the health of the network, the answer is rarely as positive as a cheap transaction suggests. Low gas prices mean there is very little competition for block space. In plain English, it means the Ethereum mainnet is quiet. While cheap fees are great for the individual user, they signal that on-chain demand for smart contract execution is subdued. The network is not necessarily "efficient"; it is simply underused. To understand why 0.1 Gwei is a signal of dormancy, you have to stop thinking of gas as a fixed fee and start seeing it as a continuous, blind auction. Every single operation on Ethereum, from a simple transfer to a complex DeFi swap, requires a certain amount of computational effort. This effort is measured in gas. Because there is a limited amount of space in each block, users must bid against each other to get their transaction included by a validator. When demand spikes, users raise their bids to ensure their transaction does not sit in the mempool for hours. This is how we reached the peaks of 500 Gwei or more during previous booms, as patentpc.com notes. When demand vanishes, validators lower the entry price to attract any available traffic. As investopedia.com explains, these fees rise and fall based on the supply and demand for transactions. At 0.1 Gwei, the "bidding war" has effectively ended because there is no one left to bid against. The official line is that Ethereum is successfully moving its activity to Layer 2 (L2) solutions. Chains like Base and Arbitrum handle the bulk of the retail traffic, then settle the final results back to the main Ethereum chain in batches. In this view, the mainnet is not a ghost town; it is a high-security settlement layer that no longer needs to be clogged with small, cheap transactions. The more skeptical read is that L2s are not just scaling Ethereum, they are eating it. If all the users, developers, and liquidity move to L2s, the mainnet loses its primary source of revenue and utility. This is the "L2 trap" mentioned by some analysts, where the main chain becomes a dormant vault while the actual ecosystem lives elsewhere. We have previously covered Ethereum layer two scaling solutions to explain this shift. The danger here is the impact on ETH's economic model. Ethereum burns a portion of the gas fees paid on every transaction. When gas is 0.1 Gwei, the burn rate drops to almost nothing. If the network does not burn enough ETH to offset the issuance of new coins to validators, ETH becomes inflationary. This contradicts the "ultrasound money" narrative that bulls have relied on for years. Currently, we see a massive disconnect. The market is greedy, and the price of ETH remains robust, but the actual use of the network is anemic. This suggests that much of the current price action is driven by speculation on centralized exchanges or institutional interest in ETFs, rather than people actually using the blockchain to build things. Despite the macro concerns, low gas is a tactical advantage for the user. If you have been avoiding the mainnet because of costs, now is the window to act. If you need to perform any of the following, do it while gas is at these levels: - Moving assets from a centralized exchange to a hardware wallet. - Interacting with older DeFi protocols that do not have L2 versions. - Minting or transferring NFTs on the main chain. - Rebalancing large portfolios across different L1 contracts. The irony of the current market is that the best time to actually use Ethereum is when the market is telling you that Ethereum is a powerhouse, but the gas data shows it is practically idling. Enjoy the cheap fees, but keep an eye on the burn rate. If the mainnet stays this quiet for too long, the "ultrasound" narrative becomes a fairy tale.

results.title: SEC Approves Listing of Bitcoin ETF Targeting 3x Daily Futures Moves
highlights: SEC Approves Listing of Bitcoin ETF Targeting 3x Daily Futures Moves A bitcoin fund targeting three times its futures benchmark’s daily performance has secured SEC listing approval. The ruling covers a broader commodity lineup and preserves exchange oversight and brokerage obligations as the sponsor pursues market access. Investors could gain amplified exposure to bitcoin futures through a newly approved listing on Cboe BZX. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) authorized the exchange rule change Oct. 2, clearing the 3x Bitcoin ETF and five companion funds sponsored by investment manager Volatility Shares LLC. The lineup also includes the 3x Ether ETF alongside gold, silver, crude oil, and natural gas offerings. Each operates as a series of VS Trust. The funds have “ETF” in their names, but legally they are exchange-traded products (ETPs) that hold commodity-linked investments. They are not regulated under the Investment Company Act of 1940, which governs conventional ETFs. The decision follows Cboe BZX’s proposal to list six leveraged commodity products, submitted Aug. 10 and published for public comment Aug. 19. The commission stated: A 1% rise in the bitcoin futures benchmark would translate into a targeted 3% daily gain before fees and expenses. A 1% decline would correspond to a targeted 3% loss. The reference portfolio’s performance can differ from changes in the cryptocurrency’s price for immediate purchase, known as its spot price. The six vehicles required individual review under exchange rules that exclude leveraged commodity-based trusts from the standard listing route. The SEC’s generic listing standards for commodity-based trust shares, approved in September 2025, allow qualifying products to list without a separate exchange rule filing. Their 3x objectives required this separate authorization. Broker recommendations remain subject to rules requiring consideration of an investor’s circumstances, potential risks, rewards, and costs. Exchange surveillance and trading-halt requirements also apply, including a halt when the daily asset valuation is not available to all market participants simultaneously. The listings remain subject to registration and operating requirements, including an effective registration statement before trading begins. Each must have at least 100,000 shares outstanding at the start of exchange trading. The sponsor must calculate net asset value per share, the value of assets minus liabilities divided by outstanding shares, daily.

None of them can actually be bought yet. On October 2, the SEC approved a Cboe BZX rule change clearing the way for six leveraged exchange-traded products built by Volatility Shares LLC, each aiming to move three times the daily price swing of its underlying asset. Two track Bitcoin and Ether. The other four track gold, silver, crude oil and natural gas. The order puts crypto, metals and energy products into the same triple-leveraged commodity ETP package, meaning one product family would let a trader bet big on an Ether candle and a barrel of crude using the same mechanics. Here's the catch almost every headline is skipping past: approval of a listing rule is not approval to trade. Cboe BZX filed the rule change on August 10, and the SEC's October 2 order just clears that exchange-level hurdle. Before any of these six funds can begin trading under its ticker, VS Trust still needs the SEC to declare its Form S-1 registration statement effective under the Securities Act of 1933, and the order sets no deadline for that. Until then, there is nothing to buy. That gap matters because it determines who's actually on the hook. Each fund is structured as a Commodity-Based Trust Share, not a registered investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940, according to the SEC order. That means these products sit outside the diversification rules, leverage limits and board oversight that apply to registered mutual funds and stock or bond ETFs. You're getting futures-based leverage wrapped in the lighter-touch commodity-trust structure that already houses products like the gold trusts, not the heavier-regulated fund category many retail investors assume covers anything with "ETF" in Volatility Shares isn't a newcomer to this corner of the market. highlights: SEC Proposes New Regulation Crypto Assets Proposed rules would create a tailored securities offering regime for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets Washington D.C., Aug. 18, 2026 — The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it proposed new rules, titled “Regulation Crypto Assets,” that would create a clear and fit-for-purpose framework for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets. This proposal follows the Commission’s March 2026 interpretation clarifying how the federal securities laws apply to certain crypto assets and transactions involving crypto assets. Together, these efforts introduce a comprehensive, tailored securities offering regime intended to address long-standing barriers to responsible capital formation and innovation within domestic crypto asset markets, while preserving the investor protections at the core of federal securities laws. “As we continue the Commission’s efforts to provide clarity for crypto markets, and as Congress works to establish a lasting regulatory framework, Regulation Crypto Assets seeks to provide crypto asset entrepreneurs and market participants with clear pathways to raise capital under the federal securities laws,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins. “In line with the Commission’s earlier interpretative guidance, this proposal would also allow for a safe harbor once an issuer has completed or permanently ceased all essential managerial efforts that it represented or promised it would take under an investment contract. Congress designed our securities laws to amplify – within specific guardrails – opportunities for entrepreneurs to innovate and build new products. Advancing this regulatory framework is a key element in our strategy to advance the rule books for the modern era and another step by the Commission to onshore innovation in crypto asset markets for generations to come.” The proposed rules include two exemptions from the registration requirements of the Securities Act of 1933 specifically tailored to certain investment contracts involving crypto assets. The first is a one-time exemption that would permit offerings of up to $5 million during a four-year period. The second exemption would permit offerings of up to $75 million during each 12-month period. Under both exemptions, issuers would be required to make certain principles-based narrative disclosures available to their investors. In addition, issuers under the second exemption would be required to provide financial statements and be subject to ongoing reporting requirements. The proposed rules also include a conditional safe harbor from the term “investment contract” in the definitions of “security” in the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. If the conditions of that proposed safe harbor are satisfied, then a crypto asset would be deemed not to be subject to an investment contract for purposes of those definitions of “security.” In addition, the proposed rules would preempt state securities law registration and qualification requirements with respect to offers and sales of securities issued pursuant to an exemption in Regulation Crypto Assets, as well as certain secondary market transactions. By building on the Commission’s interpretive guidance issued earlier this year, the proposed rules aim to bring greater clarity to when crypto assets fall within the federal securities laws, reduce incentives for issuers to create and operate offshore, and expand investment opportunities for U.S. investors with stronger, more consistent protections.
